# mediamix

<!-- badges: start -->
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/elkronos/mediamix/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/elkronos/mediamix/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
[![Lifecycle: experimental](https://img.shields.io/badge/lifecycle-experimental-orange.svg)](https://lifecycle.r-lib.org/articles/stages.html#experimental)
<!-- badges: end -->

Composable media transforms and attribution path construction for R.

mediamix turns raw marketing data into model-ready features: media spend into
carryover- and saturation-adjusted regressors, and raw event logs into
attributed customer journeys.

Use it if you fit your own marketing mix model, whether in `lm()`, `glmnet`,
`brms`, Stan or a tidymodels workflow, or if you need customer journeys and
attribution built from a raw event log.

It is a preprocessing, feature-engineering and reporting package, not a
modelling engine. `lm()`, `glmnet` and `brms` fit models better than a
marketing package would, and `tune` does hyperparameter search properly.
mediamix does the steps in front of the model and the decomposition after it,
with the methodological details that usually get skipped written into the API.

Documentation, walkthroughs and worked examples are on the package website,
<https://elkronos.github.io/mediamix/>.

## What it offers

The full MMM frameworks (Robyn in R; Meridian and PyMC-Marketing in Python)
bundle transforms, a model, an optimiser and reporting into one pipeline.
mediamix provides those pieces separately, for use around a model you choose:

- `step_adstock()` carries filter state across the train/test boundary, so
  carryover, saturation and a model penalty can be tuned jointly in one
  `tune_bayes()` call with no rows lost.
- `marginal_roi()` re-runs the whole transform on a 1% larger budget, the
  definition used by Jin et al. (2017) and by Meridian. The common shortcut,
  a curve's slope times the kernel's first weight, understates slow channels
  several-fold.
- `tune_carryover()` and, for every channel at once inside one model with
  controls, `tune_carryover_joint()` score candidates on held-out KPI with
  forward-only resampling and report the one-standard-error choice alongside
  the minimum.
- `block_bootstrap()` resamples runs of weeks to put intervals on ROI,
  marginal ROI or anything else you compute.
- `build_paths()` turns a raw event log into journeys with every construction
  choice an argument, and accounts for the conversions that filtering leaves
  unattributable.
- `attribute()` runs five rule-based credit schemes and an order-1 Markov
  removal-effect model side by side, and `attribution_spread()` reports how
  much the answer depends on the choice.
- `decay_from_half_life()` and `half_life()` translate between a decay
  coefficient and the half-life practitioners talk in, and
  `effective_window()` gives the number of periods that hold 90% of the
  effect; both halves of the package use this one vocabulary.

## Scope

| In | Out | Because |
|---|---|---|
| Adstock and saturation transforms | Model fitting | `lm`, `glmnet`, `brms` already exist |
| Carryover selection by cross-validation | Bespoke optimisers | `tune` does this properly |
| Journey construction from event logs | Higher-order Markov chains | `ChannelAttribution` does them in C++ |
| Rule-based credit and order-1 Markov removal effects | Causal incrementality | Requires experiments, not logs |
| Contribution, ROI and counterfactual marginal ROI | Budget optimisation | Deserves its own design pass |
| Media data diagnostics | Generic regression diagnostics | `broom`, `performance` |

`as_channel_paths()` exports journeys straight into `ChannelAttribution`'s
format, for higher-order models and very large path tables.

## Installation

mediamix is not yet on CRAN. Install the development version from GitHub:

```r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("elkronos/mediamix")
```

`pak` does not build vignettes for packages installed from GitHub, so
`vignette("carryover")` and the others are not available after this install.
Read them on the [package website](https://elkronos.github.io/mediamix/), or
install with `remotes::install_github("elkronos/mediamix", build_vignettes = TRUE)`.

mediamix imports `cli` and `rlang` for its messages and `data.table` for the
attribution half, where event logs get large. It has no compiled code.
`recipes`, `dials` and the rest of tidymodels are in `Suggests` and registered
conditionally, so the transforms work equally well from a Stan or `brms`
workflow that will never touch them.

## Example

### Media mix modelling

`mm_weekly` holds three years of weekly spend on five channels, with price
and revenue, for three geographies. It was simulated from known carryover and
saturation parameters, kept in its `"truth"` attribute, so every estimate
below can be checked. The example uses the north geography:

```{r}
library(mediamix)
data(mm_weekly)
truth <- attr(mm_weekly, "truth")

north <- mm_weekly[mm_weekly$geo == "north", ]
channels <- c("tv", "video", "search", "social", "display")
controls <- data.frame(week = seq_len(nrow(north)), price = north$price,
                       seasonality = north$seasonality,
                       holiday = north$holiday)
```

It is tempting to choose decay by asking which transformed series is
best-behaved. That criterion has no dependent variable in it, so it ranks
filters by how hard they smooth rather than by anything about the outcome.
`tune_carryover_joint()` scores each candidate by how well a model with every
channel and the controls predicts *held-out* revenue, so no channel is
credited with another's effect. The default model is ordinary least squares;
`fit_fn` and `predict_fn` take any other.

```{r}
joint <- tune_carryover_joint(north[channels], north$revenue,
                              controls = controls)
rbind(estimate = joint$best$decay, truth = truth$decay[channels])
```

```{r joint-facts, include = FALSE}
off <- channels[round(abs(joint$best$decay - truth$decay[channels]), 8) > 0.1]
```

Of the five, `r knitr::combine_words(off)` miss by more than 0.1. Search's
cross-validation profile is almost flat: the data does not identify its
carryover, which `plot(joint)` makes visible and a bare point estimate would
hide. Carryover is weakly identified in most real data, which is why the
one-standard-error rule (Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman, 2009) is reported
alongside, as `joint$best_1se`.

The joint search does not tune saturation, so to keep the example short the
model below uses the parameters `mm_weekly` was simulated from: geometric
adstock (Broadbent, 1979) followed by a Hill curve (Hill, 1910), which
`media_transform()` applies in that order. Any model can go on top; here it
is `lm()` with the controls. `contributions()` splits the fitted revenue into
one part per channel and a baseline, and `roi()` divides each channel's
contribution by its spend:

```{r}
one_channel <- function(ch) {
  media_transform(north[[ch]],
                  adstock = list(decay = truth$decay[[ch]]),
                  saturation = list(half_max = truth$half_max[[ch]],
                                    shape = truth$shape[[ch]]))
}
media <- as.data.frame(sapply(channels, one_channel))
fit <- lm(north$revenue ~ ., data = cbind(media, controls))
contrib <- contributions(media, fit, index = north$date)
roi(contrib, north[channels])
```

Every channel returns more than it costs on average. The main results have
`plot()` methods in one consistent, colour-vision-checked style; here is the
decomposition week by week:

```{r contributions}
plot(contrib)
```

Average ROI is a scorecard; marginal ROI is the decision variable.
`marginal_roi()` computes it the way Jin et al. (2017) and Meridian define
it, as the extra response from a 1% larger budget divided by the extra spend,
by re-running carryover and saturation rather than differentiating a curve:

```{r}
tv <- marginal_roi(north$tv, coefficient = coef(fit)[["tv"]],
                   adstock = list(decay = truth$decay[["tv"]]),
                   saturation = list(half_max = truth$half_max[["tv"]],
                                     shape = truth$shape[["tv"]]))
tv
```

```{r shortcut, include = FALSE}
z <- adstock_geometric(north$tv, decay = truth$decay[["tv"]])
shortcut <- mroi(mean(z), coefficient = coef(fit)[["tv"]],
                 half_max = truth$half_max[["tv"]],
                 shape = truth$shape[["tv"]]) * (1 - truth$decay[["tv"]])
```

Television's next pound returns `r round(tv$mroi, 2)`, close to its average
of `r round(tv$roi, 2)`. The tempting shortcut, the curve's slope times the
kernel's first weight, gives `r round(shortcut, 2)` for this channel: it
counts only the week of spend and discards the
`r round(100 * truth$decay[["tv"]])`% of the effect that arrives later.

`block_bootstrap()` puts intervals on any of these numbers. On `mm_weekly`
they are wide, which is the point: see the
[budget walkthrough](https://elkronos.github.io/mediamix/articles/budget-walkthrough.html)
for how that changes a recommendation, and how its answer compares with the
truth the data was simulated from.

### Attribution

Attribution tools such as `ChannelAttribution` consume `"a > b > c"` strings
with conversion counts attached; producing those strings is left to the
analyst. That step usually ends up as a `group_by()` and a
`paste(collapse = " > ")`, and that loses a great deal.

```{r journey-table, echo = FALSE}
data(mm_events)
ordered <- mm_events[order(mm_events$customer_id, mm_events$timestamp), ]
naive <- split(ordered$channel, ordered$customer_id)
step <- function(...) {
  s <- path_summary(suppressMessages(build_paths(
    mm_events, id = "customer_id", channel = "channel",
    timestamp = "timestamp", conversion = "conversion", ...)))
  c(s$journeys, s$mean_length)
}
steps <- rbind(
  "naive one-path-per-customer" = c(length(naive), mean(lengths(naive))),
  "split on conversion" = step(split_on = "conversion",
                               collapse_repeats = FALSE),
  "+ 30-day inactivity gap" = step(split_on = c("conversion", "gap"), gap = 30,
                                   collapse_repeats = FALSE),
  "+ collapse consecutive duplicates" = step(split_on = c("conversion", "gap"),
                                             gap = 30, collapse_repeats = TRUE)
)
more <- round(100 * (steps[4, 1] / steps[1, 1] - 1))
shorter <- round(100 * (1 - steps[4, 2] / steps[1, 2]))
```

On `mm_events`, the package's
`r format(nrow(mm_events), big.mark = ",")`-event synthetic log:

```{r journey-table-print, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  ` ` = rownames(steps),
  journeys = format(steps[, 1], big.mark = ","),
  `mean length` = sprintf("%.2f", steps[, 2]),
  check.names = FALSE
), align = c("l", "r", "r"), row.names = FALSE)
```

The last row has `r more`% more journeys than the first, and they are
`r shorter`% shorter. Journey counts and lengths feed a Markov transition
matrix directly, so those are not rounding differences. Each of these choices
is an argument to `build_paths()`:

```{r}
paths <- build_paths(
  mm_events,
  id = "customer_id", channel = "channel", timestamp = "timestamp",
  conversion = "conversion", value = "value",
  lookback = 30,                       # or read it off conversion_lag()
  split_on = c("conversion", "gap"), gap = 30,
  collapse_repeats = TRUE,
  keep_null_paths = TRUE,              # Markov removal effects need these
  direct = "label"
)
```

`build_paths()` handles the things that go wrong between an event log and a
set of journeys: journey splitting, lookback windows, non-converting paths,
direct, none and missing channels, consecutive duplicates, duplicate events,
timestamps that do not parse, deterministic tie-breaking, and accounting for
conversions that filtering leaves unattributable. Each is an argument, not an
assumption.

Dropping direct traffic can strip a converting journey of every touchpoint it
had. mediamix fixes the conversion facts before any filtering, so those
conversions are counted and reported as `conversions_unattributable` rather
than quietly shrinking the denominator.

Any single credit rule gives you a number. Several give you the range that
number could have been. `attribute()` runs five heuristic rules and an order-1
Markov removal-effect model (Anderl et al., 2016). The four channels whose
share varies most:

```{r}
shares <- attribute(paths)
spread <- attribution_spread(shares)
head(spread, 4)
```

```{r attribution}
plot(shares)
```

```{r spread-facts, include = FALSE}
display <- spread[spread$channel == "display", ]
heuristic <- shares[shares$rule != "markov", ]
markov <- shares[shares$rule == "markov", ]
inside <- vapply(markov$channel, function(ch) {
  h <- heuristic$share[heuristic$channel == ch]
  m <- markov$share[markov$channel == ch]
  m >= min(h) && m <= max(h)
}, logical(1))
```

Display's share runs from `r round(100 * display$min_share)`% to
`r round(100 * display$max_share)`% depending only on the convention chosen.
That channel has not been measured; it has been assigned a number. The Markov
share falls inside the heuristic range for `r sum(inside)` of
`r length(inside)` channels here: a data-driven convention narrows the
argument without ending it.

Rule-based attribution is a bookkeeping convention, not a causal estimate. It
divides observed conversions among observed touchpoints by a rule you chose; it
cannot tell you what would have happened if a channel had not run, because that
outcome is not in the log. Only an experiment answers that.

## Where to go next

From first steps to deeper material:

- `vignette("mediamix")`: getting started, from raw data to contributions and
  ROI.
- The [budget walkthrough](https://elkronos.github.io/mediamix/articles/budget-walkthrough.html):
  one budget question from weekly spend to a recommendation, checked against
  the parameters the data was simulated from.
- `vignette("carryover")`: choosing decay and lag by cross-validation, and
  why five correlated channels make it harder.
- `vignette("tidymodels")`: joint tuning of transform and model parameters,
  with recipe steps that carry adstock across the train/test boundary.
- `vignette("journeys")`: building journeys from event logs.
- `vignette("spine")`: carryover and credit are the same idea, the geometric
  kernel run forward from spend for adstock and backward from a conversion
  for time-decay credit.
- [Methods and references](https://elkronos.github.io/mediamix/articles/methodology.html):
  the method behind each function and where it comes from.
- [How mediamix relates to other tools](https://elkronos.github.io/mediamix/articles/comparison.html):
  Robyn, Meridian, PyMC-Marketing and ChannelAttribution.

The walkthrough, the methods page and the comparison are on the website only;
the vignettes also ship with the package.
